source_title: Notifications for Wayland that look like they belong on a computer from this decade. Drawn with Rune. - GitHub
source_excerpt:
A control center for Wayland that looks like it belongs on a computer from this decade.
Hokum is one app for compositors with zwlr_layer_shell_v1 (niri, sway, Hyprland, river and others), drawn with Rune , our Rust UI framework:
Notifications: a freedesktop notification daemon ( org.freedesktop.Notifications ) whose cards slide in, restack on springs and get out of the way.
Sound: output, input and the apps playing, on PipeWire. Devices, ports, Bluetooth codecs and balance a row down; profiles, virtual outputs, routing and the clock in the pane beside them.
Bluetooth: power, connected and paired devices with battery, on BlueZ. Pairing (codes inline), trust, rename and forget a row down; adapters and raw properties in the pane beside them.
One window holds all three, one section each. One tray icon opens a panel with the output's volume and device, the microphone while something records, your Bluetooth devices and Do not disturb.

With Nix, try it with nix run github:anomalyco/hokum . On NixOS, add the flake as an input and install it so D-Bus activation and the user unit find it:
Or download the hokum executable from Releases and install it on your PATH together with the systemd unit, D-Bus activation file and launcher entry from packaging/ . Development builds of dev are on the dev channel .
Hokum starts through D-Bus activation on the first notification. To start it with your session instead, and stop another daemon (mako, dunst, swaync) holding the name:
The first time it runs, Hokum shows one welcome card of its own with a button into Settings. It remembers that in ~/.local/state/hokum/welcomed .
Sound needs PipeWire (with WirePlumber) and Bluetooth needs BlueZ; without them their sections say so in one line and the tray panel leaves them out. The packages depend on libpipewire and recommend pipewire , wireplumber and bluez .
Hokum runs on compositors with layer-shell: niri, sway, Hyprland, river and others, and KDE Plasma. It doesn't run on GNOME, which has no layer-shell to draw cards with; there it says so and exits.
Some desktop shells are the notification server themselves rather than a separate daemon, and they never let another one take the name, --replace included: turn off the shell's own notifications first, then start Hokum.
KDE Plasma: System Tray settings → Entries → Notifications: Disabled (or remove the Notifications widget), then systemctl --user enable --now hokum.service . If Plasma still holds the name, log out and back in.
When a shell keeps the name, Hokum says which one and what to do, and exits with status 78, which hokum.service doesn't restart on.
dismiss , invoke and dnd are for keybindings and bars, like makoctl . hokum dnd on saves to config.kdl just as the settings window's switch does. They call app.hokum.Daemon on the session bus ( Dismiss , Invoke , SetDoNotDisturb and a DoNotDisturb property that announces its changes), which scripts can use directly.
Like Hex, Hokum is one process: the service owns the bus name, draws the cards on a click-through overlay, hosts the window, runs Sound and Bluetooth on their own threads and keeps the tray icon. Launching hokum again shows that window. A module that can't start, or fails later, says so in its section and leaves the rest running.
Sound and Bluetooth are on unless config.kdl turns them off; the end of each section's advanced pane has a button for it too. With both off there's no tray icon.
When the default output's volume or mute changes from outside Hokum (volume keys, wpctl , an app), one Volume card shows the level and updates in place; it shows through Do not disturb. A Brightness card does the same when the screen's backlight changes. When a paired Bluetooth device connects, a card says so with its battery, and one more warns once when a device's battery drops below 20 % (again only after it's been back above 30 %). Turn them off with osd #false , brightness #false and bluetooth-notifications #false in modules .
Hokum registers a BlueZ pairing agent, so pairings started from Hokum prompt in Hokum, with the code under the device. It asks to be the default agent (the one that answers pairings a device starts, and untrusted devices asking for a service) only when no other Bluetooth app that keeps one is running (blueman's applet, blueberry, Plasma's Bluedevil); then those keep answering them.
One config file: ~/.config/hokum/config.kdl starts from a theme and overrides anything: look ( tokens ), layout ( template ), per-app and per-text rule s, behaviour and modules (which only the config sets; themes are just looks). The settings window edits the same file, keeping your comments, and hand edits apply as you save. See docs/theming.md .
Themes: eight built in (Soft, Crisp, Capsule, Ribbon, Terminal, Bubble, Signal, Pill), shown in a gallery as real cards, plus Omarchy on Omarchy, which follows its current theme's colours. Capsule, with app icons, is the default. Custom themes are written by your coding agent: the settings window gives you a prompt that points it at hokum.app (the same guide as docs/themes.md ), the complete guide to the format. A Rhai script can rewrite or drop notifications too.
Per app: mute, how long its cards stay, and breaking through Do not disturb, for every app that has sent you a notification.
Icons and pictures: app icons from your icon theme (the one your desktop set: GNOME's, KDE's or GTK's setting), found from whatever names the app: its icon, its desktop-entry , its Flatpak, Snap, AppImage or systemd app unit, or its name. A browser's notification from an installed web app ( --app=https://… launchers, Omarchy's and Linux Mint's) shows as that app. The pictures notifications carry (avatars, album art) show beside the text, unless the picture is just the app's icon again. Emoji draw in colour.
Behaviour: screen corner, how long cards stay, how many show, pause while hovered, and Do not disturb (only critical notifications and apps you allow show).
Sounds (opt-in): behaviour { sound #true } plays a sound for new cards, with its own for critical ones and per-app rule s; apps' sound-file , sound-name and suppress-sound hints count. See docs/theming.md .
Cards: action buttons, a click for the default action (with an XDG activation token, so the app can raise its window on Wayland), a right-click to dismiss, progress bars ( value ), and in-place replacement by x-dunst-stack-tag / x-canonical-private-synchronous (volume, brightness). Critical notifications stay until dismissed. Slack's [workspace] in #channel titles become the sender, the message, and the channel beside the app's name. Omarchy's click commands, buttons and glyphs work too.
Hokum keeps config.kdl , your themes/ and script.rhai in ~/.config/hokum/ , and notices when any of them change.
Hokum never updates itself without a click. A minute after it starts, and then hourly (every 30 minutes on dev builds), the service fetches its channel's release manifest ( https://anoma.ly/release/hokum/desktop/ .json , sent as hokum/ / ). When the published executable for your machine differs from the running one (compared by sha256), one Hokum card says so:
Installed as a plain file you can write ( ~/.local/bin/hokum ): Update downloads it, checks its size and sha256, replaces the executable and restarts Hokum, which then says "Hokum updated". If anything fails, the card says what and the old executable stays.
Installed by a package manager (AUR, .deb, .rpm): the button copies the command that updates it ( paru -Syu hokum-bin , for instance) with wl-copy , or opens hokum.app.
Dismiss the card and that build stays quiet until Hokum restarts or a day passes. Like Hokum's other cards it waits out Do not disturb. Failures are silent and retried at the next check. To turn checks off, set check-for-updates #false in behaviour in config.kdl . Builds run from a cargo target/ folder never check. hokum update checks now; hokum update --install does what the card's button does.
Needs the PipeWire headers and clang for bindgen ( pipewire and clang on Arch; libpipewire-0.3-dev libspa-0.2-dev clang libclang-dev pkg-config on Debian and Ubuntu).
HOKUM_SOUND_BACKEND=mock and HOKUM_BLUETOOTH_BACKEND=mock run the service on fake devices.
Releases are cut by .github/workflows/release.yml ; see docs/releasing.md .
